A.explanation: Total wire drop is $1.5 \text{ V}$ for $2.50 \text{ A}$, giving $0.30 \text{ }\Omega$ per wire, which gives $L \approx 10.6 \text{ m}$ from $R=\rho L/A$.

B.explanation: This is twice the cable length because the total wire length $2L$ was used as $L$ in $R=\rho L/A$.

C.explanation: This uses the full $12.0 \text{ V}$ or lamp $10.5 \text{ V}$ instead of the $1.5 \text{ V}$ lost in the connecting wires.

D.explanation: This combines using the full supply voltage and forgetting to divide the total wire resistance between the two wires.

hints: Notice the supply is $12.0 \text{ V}$ but only $10.5 \text{ V}$ reaches the lamp, so find how much potential difference is left for the two connecting wires.
Connect that lost potential difference and the $2.50 \text{ A}$ current to resistance with $V=IR$, remembering the $1.5 \text{ V}$ is shared by two wires of length $L$.
Use $R=\rho L/A$ for one wire with $\rho = 1.70 \times 10^{-8} \text{ }\Omega \text{ m}$ and $A = 6.00 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}^2$ to solve for $L$.
walkthrough: The wires take potential difference from the lamp. Lost p.d. in both wires $= 12.0 - 10.5 = 1.5 \text{ V}$.
The same $2.50 \text{ A}$ flows through the two wires in series, so total wire resistance $R_{total} = V/I = 1.5/2.50 = 0.60 \text{ }\Omega$.
The cable has two identical wires each of length $L$, so resistance of one wire is $R = 0.60/2 = 0.30 \text{ }\Omega$.
For one wire, $R = \rho L/A$, so $L = RA/\rho$.
